title: Composing MIDI Tricks
intro: Getting ideas out of your head and into the sequencer before they evaporate. These tricks are about speed of capture first and correctness second — you can always fix it later, but you cannot un‑forget an idea.

tips.t: Musical Typing turns your laptop into a synth
tips.d: ⌘K opens a playable keyboard mapped to your QWERTY keys. Z and X shift octaves, C and V shift velocity, and the tab key holds sustain. No controller required.

tips.t: Capture the last thing you played, even when not recording
tips.d: If you played something great while the transport was rolling but not recording, hit ⇧R and Logic writes it to a region retroactively. MIDI works on any recent version. Audio needs Logic 11.2 or later, and the audio track has to be record-enabled with the transport playing — Logic can only hand back what it was already buffering.

tips.t: Record MIDI while the transport is stopped
tips.d: Logic's MIDI buffer is always listening. Even with the transport parked, Flashback Capture will grab what you just played — notes and controller moves both.

tips.t: Use the Step Input Keyboard for parts you cannot play
tips.d: Window > Show Step Input Keyboard. Enter notes one at a time at an exact rhythmic value. Complex parts get entered accurately without a single quantise pass.

tips.t: Draw notes with the Pencil, delete with the Eraser
tips.d: The Pencil creates notes at the current division. To remove one, double-click it with the Pointer or switch to the Eraser tool. ⌥-drag any note to duplicate it at the same pitch.

tips.t: New notes inherit the last note you touched
tips.d: There is no default-velocity field. A note you draw takes the velocity and length of the last note you selected or edited — so set one hi-hat to 70, then draw the rest and they follow.

tips.t: Use the Chord Trigger MIDI plugin to play chords with one finger
tips.d: Insert Chord Trigger in the MIDI FX slot, hit Learn, play a chord, then assign it to a single key. Whole progressions become one‑finger performances.

tips.t: Force everything into key with Transposer's scale quantize
tips.d: Insert the Transposer MIDI FX and turn on its scale quantize, then pick your root and scale. Every wrong note you play is bent to the nearest right one in real time.

tips.t: Use Arpeggiator to generate parts, then commit them
tips.d: Insert Arpeggiator and dial in a pattern, then use Bounce in Place — or record its output to another track — to turn the live effect into editable notes.

tips.t: Transpose without touching the notes
tips.d: Select a region and use the Region inspector's Transpose field. It is non‑destructive, so you can audition a key change for the whole song in seconds.

tips.t: Transpose only the notes, permanently
tips.d: Select notes in the Piano Roll and transpose with the Transpose key commands: ⌥↑ and ⌥↓ by semitone, ⇧⌥↑ and ⇧⌥↓ by octave. Plain arrow keys move the selection, they do not transpose.

tips.t: Use the Modifier MIDI plugin to remap anything to anything
tips.d: Turn modwheel into aftertouch, velocity into CV, or pitchbend into expression without leaving Logic.

tips.t: Double a part an octave down without a second track
tips.d: Insert the Transposer MIDI plugin on a duplicate of the region's track, or simply select the notes, ⌥‑drag them down an octave and lower their velocity by 20.

groups.heading: Working fast while ideas are hot

tips.t: Record into a cycle with take folders
tips.d: Set the cycle, arm the track, and let it loop. With MIDI cycle recording set to create take folders, every pass is a separate take you can swap between later.

tips.t: Merge takes when you are layering, not replacing
tips.d: For building up a drum pattern one element per pass, set MIDI cycle recording to Merge instead. Each loop adds to the same region.

tips.t: Use Replace mode to punch over a bad bar
tips.d: Enable Replace in the transport and record over a section — the old MIDI in that range is removed rather than layered on top.

tips.t: Name the region before you move on
tips.d: Select the region and press ⇧N to rename it, or use the Text tool or the Region inspector. Twenty untitled regions in a week's time is a genuinely expensive mistake.

tips.t: Use ⌘D to duplicate an instrument track with all its settings
tips.d: Instant second layer with the same patch, ready to be detuned, transposed or re‑voiced.

tips.t: Freeze the instrument as soon as the part is done
tips.d: Click the Freeze button in the track header to render the software instrument to audio. Your CPU comes back and the part is locked in.

tips.t: Drag a MIDI region onto an audio track to bounce it instantly
tips.d: Logic renders it through the instrument and its plugins. It is the fastest way to commit an idea to audio.

tips.t: Keep one “sketch” instrument track loaded at all times
tips.d: A piano patch on a permanently armed track means any idea is three seconds from being captured. The moment capture takes effort, ideas stop arriving.

tips.t: Use Note Repeat for hi‑hats and rolls
tips.d: Enable Note Repeat in the Step Sequencer or from the drum pad controls and hold a note to generate a perfectly timed roll at the current division.

tips.t: Humanise deliberately with the Randomise function
tips.d: Select notes, then Functions > MIDI Transform > Humanize in the Piano Roll. Set small values for position and velocity — 5 to 10 ticks is plenty.
